summary.text: A storm is any disturbed state of the natural environment or of the atmosphere of an astronomical body, marked by things like strong wind, hail, lightning or heavy rain and snow.
Storms form when a centre of low pressure develops with high pressure around it, and this clash of opposing forces drives winds and builds clouds such as cumulonimbus.
They can harm lives and property through storm surge, flooding, lightning and wind shear, yet long rainy systems also ease drought where they pass.

facts.label: Blizzard snowfall rate
facts.value: At least 5 cm (2 in) per hour

items.prompt: On a scorching afternoon, hot air rises off a bare field and a small spinning column of dust appears. What set it off?

options.label: A huge high-pressure system moving in
A small local low-pressure area from rising hot air
Cold air sinking from a passing thundercloud
Moisture freezing as it falls through cold air

items.explain: Hot air rising off hot ground can form small localized low-pressure areas, which produce little disturbances like dust devils and whirlwinds.

items.prompt: Rain is falling, the air near the ground is below freezing, but a thick warm layer sits higher up. Roads turn to glass. What kind of storm is this?

options.label: A blizzard
A hailstorm
An ice storm
A dust storm

items.explain: In an ice storm, rain falls into the freezing surface layer and freezes on impact into a glaze, making unheated roads too slick to drive.

items.prompt: A farming region has had no proper rain for months. A slow, soaking storm system then crawls across it for days. What is the most likely upside?

options.label: It helps relieve the drought
It lowers the risk of any flooding
It stops the ground from eroding
It cools the region for the season

items.explain: Systems with significant rainfall and duration help alleviate drought in the places they move through.

items.prompt: A huge forest fire grows so intense that it starts making its own strong winds, which feed the flames further. What is this called?

options.label: A microburst
A derecho
A squall
A firestorm

items.explain: Firestorms are fires so intense that they create and sustain their own wind systems, most often during the largest bush and forest fires.

items.prompt: In the US today, a storm brings gale-force winds and heavy snow piling up 6 cm an hour, but the air is only around −3 °C. Could it still count as a blizzard there?

options.label: No, it must be colder than −10 °C
Yes, the cold requirement has largely been dropped
No, blizzards need wind but no falling snow
Only if it lasts for at least a full day

items.explain: Blizzards were generally tied to very cold conditions, but the temperature criterion has lately fallen out of the definition across the United States.

items.prompt: Out at sea, the sustained wind reaches about 55 mph. A ship's captain hears the forecast simply call it "a storm". What can such a system do?

options.label: Only threaten small boats near the shore
Nothing serious unless lightning strikes
Sink vessels of every type and size
Only slow ships down without real risk

items.explain: Sea storms have sustained winds of 48 knots (55 mph) or more and can sink vessels of all types and sizes.

pack.title: When the Sky Pushes Back
pack.question: What makes a storm, and how do different storms harm us?

beats.title: When the Sky Pushes Back
beats.hook: Less than a centimetre of ice can be enough to start bringing down power lines.

beats.prompt: A centre of low pressure forms, ringed by a system of high pressure. What tends to happen next?
beats.explain: This combination of opposing forces creates winds and can form storm clouds such as cumulonimbus.

choices.label: The pressure differences cancel out at once
choices.feedback: The opposing forces do not simply cancel; their clash is what drives the weather.

choices.label: Only the temperature drops, with no wind
choices.feedback: Cooling alone is not the result described; the clash produces winds.

choices.label: Winds pick up and storm clouds can build
The air goes still and skies clear
choices.feedback: Calm skies sound right for high pressure, but here the two systems push against each other.

beats.prompt: Match each storm to what defines it

right.label: A very powerful thunderstorm wind lasting minutes
Winds lift sand or soil, cutting visibility
A fire makes its own wind system

beats.explain: Each storm type is defined by its main disruption: ice, airborne soil, fire-driven wind or a brief powerful gust.

beats.prompt: Sort each into harm storms can cause or benefit they can bring
beats.explain: Storms damage lives and property through surge, flooding and blocked roads, while long rainy systems ease drought and heavy snow allows winter sports.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?

steps.text: Freezing rain coats everything in a glaze of ice.
About 8 mm of ice, especially with a breeze, can start downing power lines.
So ice storms only trouble small rural towns.
Unheated roads also become too slick to drive on.

beats.explain: Ice storms can cripple small towns and large metropolitan cities alike.

beats.idea: Storms grow from low pressure surrounded by high pressure, and each kind does its damage in its own way: wind, ice, snow, hail or water.
